lessons.title: Producers, consumers and decomposers: who eats who
lessons.curriculum_text: explain the roles and interactions of consumers, producers and decomposers within a habitat and how food chains represent feeding relationships
lessons.intro: Every mangrove, riverbank and backyard around Cooktown is full of living things with a job to do. Let's find out what those jobs are, and how a food chain shows who eats who.

sections.heading: Producers: the food makers
sections.body:
A **producer** is a living thing that makes its own food. Plants are producers. They use sunlight, water and air to make food inside their leaves. This is called **photosynthesis**.

Around Cooktown, mango trees, seagrass meadows and mangrove trees are all producers. They don't need to eat anything else to survive. Every food chain starts with a producer, because producers are the only living things that can turn sunlight into food energy.

sections.heading: Consumers: the eaters
sections.body:
A **consumer** is a living thing that eats other living things for energy, because it cannot make its own food.

- A **herbivore** eats only plants. A cassowary eating fallen rainforest fruit is a herbivore.
- A **carnivore** eats only other animals. A saltwater crocodile ambushing a fish is a carnivore.
- An **omnivore** eats both plants and animals. Humans are usually omnivores.

Consumers get their energy second-hand, by eating something that already has energy stored in it.

example.prompt: A goanna eats a small lizard. Is the goanna a producer or a consumer, and why?
working: The goanna cannot make its own food from sunlight
It gets energy by eating another animal
example.answer: A consumer, because it eats other living things for energy

sections.heading: Decomposers: nature's recyclers
sections.body:
A **decomposer** breaks down dead plants and animals into simpler nutrients. Fungi, bacteria and some crabs and worms are decomposers.

In the mangroves along the Endeavour River, fallen leaves pile up in the mud every day. Fungi, bacteria and mud crabs slowly break that leaf litter down. This releases nutrients back into the mud, which mangrove trees then use to grow. Without decomposers, dead material would just pile up forever and nutrients would never get recycled.

sections.heading: Reading a food chain
sections.body:
A **food chain** is drawn as a line of living things joined by arrows. The arrow means "energy flows to", so it points from what gets eaten to what eats it.

A simple Endeavour River food chain looks like this: algae → small fish → barramundi → crocodile. Algae is the producer at the start. Each arrow after that points to a consumer that gets its energy by eating the thing before it.

example.prompt: Put these into a correct food chain, starting with the producer: crocodile, algae, small fish, barramundi.
working: A food chain always starts with a producer
Each next link eats the one before it

key_points: Producers, like mango trees and seagrass, make their own food using sunlight.
Herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat animals, and omnivores eat both.
Decomposers like fungi and bacteria break down dead material and recycle nutrients.
A food chain's arrows show the direction energy flows, from producer to consumer.
Every food chain starts with a producer.
lessons.try_this: Grab some paper and draw or write out a food chain from your own backyard or a place you know well, such as: grass → grasshopper → gecko → cat. Cut the words into cards, mix them up, then race a family member to put them back in the correct order with the producer first.

questions.prompt: Producers make their own food using sunlight.
questions.explain: Producers, like plants, use sunlight, water and air to make their own food through photosynthesis. That's what makes them producers rather than consumers.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a decomposer?
choices: Fungi growing on a fallen log
A mango tree
A cassowary
A saltwater crocodile
questions.answer: Fungi growing on a fallen log
questions.explain: Fungi break down dead plants and animals into nutrients, which makes them decomposers. The mango tree is a producer, and the cassowary and crocodile are consumers.

questions.prompt: In the chain algae → small fish → barramundi, a bad wet season kills off most of the small fish. What would you expect to happen to the barramundi soon after, and why?
choices: They would likely struggle, because their main food source has dropped
They would be fine, because barramundi make their own food like a producer
They would turn into decomposers to survive
The algae would start eating the barramundi instead
questions.answer: They would likely struggle, because their main food source has dropped
questions.explain: Barramundi are consumers - they get energy by eating other living things, so losing the small fish they eat removes their main energy source, which can hurt their numbers.

questions.prompt: A cassowary spends its whole day eating fallen rainforest fruit and never eats meat. What one word describes this kind of diet?
questions.explain: An animal that eats only plants, like a cassowary eating fruit, is called a herbivore.

questions.prompt: Fallen mango leaves pile up under a backyard tree for months, yet the pile never grows as tall as you'd expect from a whole wet season of leaf drop. What is most likely happening to the missing leaf litter?
choices: Fungi, bacteria and other decomposers are breaking it down and returning nutrients to the soil
The leaves are evaporating into water vapour
Herbivores are eating all of the fallen leaves whole
The leaves are turning directly into new mango trees
questions.answer: Fungi, bacteria and other decomposers are breaking it down and returning nutrients to the soil
questions.explain: Decomposers constantly break down dead plant material, recycling its nutrients into the soil, which is why leaf litter doesn't just keep piling up forever.

questions.prompt: A food chain diagram lists these: mangrove leaves, fungus, mud crab, egret, python. How many of these are consumers (not counting the producer or the decomposer)?
questions.explain: Mangrove leaves are the producer and fungus is a decomposer. Mud crab, egret and python all get energy by eating other living things, so those three are the consumers.

questions.prompt: If every decomposer disappeared from a habitat, dead leaves and animals would stop breaking down, but the nutrients trapped inside them would still find their own way back into the soil for plants to use.
questions.explain: Without decomposers, nutrients stay locked inside dead material - they don't get back into the soil by themselves. Decomposers are the only living things that release those nutrients so producers can use them again.

questions.prompt: Small fish eat algae, and crocodiles eat small fish. Which food chain below correctly shows this, with each arrow meaning 'is eaten by'?
choices: Crocodile → small fish → algae
Algae → small fish → crocodile
Small fish → algae → crocodile
Algae → crocodile → small fish
questions.answer: Algae → small fish → crocodile
questions.explain: A food chain starts with the producer (algae) and each arrow points to whatever eats the thing before it, ending with the small fish being eaten by the crocodile.

questions.prompt: A drought kills most of the grass in a paddock. Grasshoppers eat the grass, and lizards eat the grasshoppers. If the grasshopper population drops sharply because of the drought, what is most likely to happen to the lizard population?
questions.explain: Lizards get their energy from grasshoppers. Fewer grasshoppers means less food for lizards, so the lizard population is likely to decrease as well, not stay the same.

questions.prompt: In a pond food chain, algae feed tadpoles, tadpoles are eaten by fish, and fish are eaten by a heron. A biologist counts 40 tadpoles, and each fish needs to eat 8 tadpoles to survive to adulthood. If every tadpole gets eaten, how many fish could this tadpole population support?
questions.explain: Divide the total tadpoles by how many each fish needs: 40 tadpoles divided by 8 per fish equals 5 fish supported by this food source.

questions.prompt: Mud crabs help decompose fallen mangrove leaves, but overharvesting removes almost all the mud crabs from one stretch of river. Predict what would happen to the leaf litter on the mangrove floor there.
questions.explain: Mud crabs are one of the decomposers breaking down leaf litter. With far fewer crabs doing that job, dead leaves would build up faster than they're broken down.

questions.prompt: A hawk mainly eats snakes, snakes mainly eat rats, and rats mainly eat grain. A disease wipes out most of the rats. Which best describes the most likely knock-on effect two steps away from the rats?
choices: Grain increases and hawks may struggle to find enough food
Hawks increase in number immediately
Grain decreases sharply
Snakes increase in number
questions.answer: Grain increases and hawks may struggle to find enough food
questions.explain: With fewer rats, less grain gets eaten, so grain increases. Snakes also lose their main food source, so their numbers can fall, which then leaves hawks with less to eat too. Both effects ripple two steps from the rats.

activity.title: Habitat survey: find every link in a food chain
activity.why: Finding real evidence of producers, consumers and decomposers outside proves they can spot food chain roles in real life, not just name them on a worksheet.
materials: notebook and pencil
a magnifying glass if you have one
a small stick for gently checking leaf litter
steps: Choose an outdoor spot to explore for 15 minutes, such as your yard, a park or a nature strip. Stay well away from any water's edge.
Walk slowly and count how many different KINDS of plants (producers) you can see, such as trees, grasses or weeds.
Look for evidence of consumers: chewed leaves, insect bites, feathers, droppings, spider webs, or the animals themselves. Count how many separate pieces of evidence you find.
Look for evidence of decomposers: fungi, mould, or rotting wood or leaves. Count how many separate signs you find.
Pick the single most interesting piece of evidence you found and note what role (producer, consumer or decomposer) it shows.
Record your counts and write a few sentences describing that best piece of evidence and which role it plays in a food chain.

record.label: How many different kinds of plants (producers) did you spot?
record.hint: count the different kinds, not every single plant

record.label: How many separate signs of decomposers (fungi, mould, rotting wood) did you find?
Describe the single most interesting piece of evidence you found, and which food chain role it shows.
Where did you do your survey?

activity.check: A believable result is usually 3 to 15 kinds of plants and at least a couple of decomposer signs like fungi or rotting leaves. The written description should name one specific real thing they saw, not a generic answer copied from the lesson.

lessons.title: Food webs: what happens when one link disappears
lessons.curriculum_text: explain the roles and interactions of consumers, producers and decomposers within a habitat and how food chains represent feeding relationships
lessons.intro: Real habitats are messier than one neat food chain. Most animals eat more than one thing, which links chains together into a food web. Let's see what happens when one link in that web disappears.

sections.heading: From chains to webs
sections.body:
A single food chain only shows one path of energy, like algae → fish → crocodile. But in real life, a crocodile doesn't only eat one kind of fish, and that fish doesn't only eat one kind of insect.

When you connect all the overlapping food chains in one habitat together, you get a **food web**. A food web is a much more realistic picture of how energy actually moves through a place, because it shows every feeding connection at once.

sections.heading: A Cooktown food web
sections.body:
Imagine a food web around the Endeavour River and nearby mangroves. Producers like seagrass, algae and mangrove leaves are eaten by mud crabs, small fish and insects. Those are eaten by bigger fish, birds like egrets, goannas and pythons. Crocodiles sit near the top, eating fish, birds and sometimes other animals.

Many of these animals share the same food, and many predators eat more than one kind of prey. That's what makes it a web instead of a single line.

sections.heading: What happens when a link is removed
sections.body:
Every living thing in a food web is connected to several others. If one species disappears or its numbers drop sharply, the effects usually spread outward.

- Animals that used to eat it may struggle to find enough food.
- Animals it used to eat may suddenly increase, because nothing is controlling their numbers.
- These changes can then affect other species further along the web, even ones that never directly interacted with the missing species.

example.prompt: If mud crabs almost disappeared from a mangrove food web, what would most likely happen to the fish, birds and crocodiles that eat them?
working: Mud crabs are a food source for several predators
Removing that food source doesn't add a new one
example.answer: They would have less food available and their numbers could drop

sections.heading: Cane toads: a real Far North Queensland example
sections.body:
Cane toads are an **invasive species** in Far North Queensland, meaning they were introduced and are not naturally part of the local food web. Cane toads carry a poison strong enough to kill many native predators, such as goannas, quolls and some snakes, when the predators try to eat them.

When these predators die from eating toxic toads, they are removed from the food web. That can allow the animals those predators used to hunt, such as insects or small reptiles, to increase, because one of their natural controls is gone.

key_points: A food web is made up of many overlapping, connected food chains.
Most animals eat more than one kind of food, which links chains together.
Removing one species from a food web affects the animals connected to it, and can ripple further outward.
Cane toads are an invasive species whose poison kills native predators like goannas, disrupting local food webs.
A change to one part of a food web rarely stays isolated to just that one part.
lessons.try_this: On paper, draw 6 to 8 animals and plants from a habitat you know, such as a garden or the bush near home. Draw arrows connecting what eats what. Then pick one animal and cover it with your hand. Talk through with a family member what might happen to the other animals connected to it.

questions.prompt: A food web shows only one path of energy through a habitat.
questions.explain: A food web shows many overlapping food chains connected together, not just one path. A single path is a food chain, not a food web.

questions.prompt: What is a food web made of?
choices: Many connected food chains
A single food chain
Only decomposers
Only producers
questions.answer: Many connected food chains
questions.explain: A food web forms when several overlapping food chains in a habitat are connected together, because most animals eat more than one kind of food.

questions.prompt: Cane toads spread into a goanna's habitat for the first time. Some goannas try eating the toads, which are poisonous to them. What is the most likely effect on the goanna population over the next few years?
choices: It can shrink, because some goannas are poisoned when they eat toxic toads
It grows quickly, because toads make an excellent new food source
It stays exactly the same, because goannas avoid all new species
It shifts entirely to eating mangrove leaves instead
questions.answer: It can shrink, because some goannas are poisoned when they eat toxic toads
questions.explain: Cane toads carry a poison strong enough to kill goannas that try to eat them, so a population can decline sharply after toads arrive.

questions.prompt: Cane toads were brought to Australia from overseas and are not naturally part of any local food web here. What term describes a species like this?
questions.explain: A species introduced to a place it doesn't naturally belong, which can disrupt the existing food web, is called an invasive species.

questions.prompt: Mud crabs in a mangrove food web are eaten by fish, birds and crocodiles. One year, overfishing sharply reduces the mud crab population. What is the most likely knock-on effect?
choices: The predators that ate crabs now have less food available
The mangrove trees stop producing leaves entirely
Nothing changes for any other species in the food web
Decomposers stop breaking down dead material
questions.answer: The predators that ate crabs now have less food available
questions.explain: Mud crabs are a food source for several predators. Removing that food source means those predators must find other food or their numbers may drop too.

questions.prompt: A food web diagram shows 5 producers and 11 consumers connected to them, plus 2 decomposers. How many living things are shown in total, not counting the decomposers?
questions.explain: Add the producers and consumers only: 5 producers plus 11 consumers equals 16 living things, since the question asks to exclude decomposers.

questions.prompt: In a food web, an animal can be affected by the disappearance of a species it never directly ate or was eaten by.
questions.explain: Effects can spread indirectly through connected links in a web. Even species with no direct feeding connection to what's missing can be affected as changes ripple outward.

questions.prompt: A pond has 3 kinds of producers. Each producer is eaten by 4 different kinds of consumer, and no consumer eats more than one kind of producer. How many separate feeding connections does this make in total?
questions.explain: 3 producers times 4 consumers each gives 12 separate feeding connections. A real food web has many overlapping connections like this, which is what makes it a web rather than a single chain.

questions.prompt: Cane toads killed off most of the goannas in an area. Goannas used to hunt many small skinks. Predict what is likely to happen to the skink population now that far fewer goannas are hunting them.
questions.explain: Goannas were a predator controlling skink numbers. With most goannas gone, one of the skinks' main threats has been removed, so their population is likely to increase.

questions.prompt: Six different predators in a food web each rely on mud crabs for about a quarter (25%) of their diet. If mud crabs completely disappeared, roughly what percentage of these predators' total diet would they now need to replace from other prey?
questions.explain: If mud crabs make up 25% of a predator's diet, losing mud crabs entirely means that predator needs to find another food source to replace that same 25% share.

questions.prompt: Two bird species both eat the same insect, and frogs also eat that insect. A pesticide wipes out that one insect species. Even though the pesticide never touched the frogs directly, they would have less ____ available.
questions.explain: The frogs are connected to the pesticide's effect indirectly, through the food web. Losing the shared insect removes one of the frogs' food sources, even though nothing touched the frogs themselves.

questions.prompt: A cyclone destroys most of the seagrass in a bay. Dugongs eat seagrass directly, and tiger sharks sometimes eat dugongs. Which best describes the most likely ripple effect through this food web?
choices: Dugongs would have less food, and this could eventually reduce food available to tiger sharks
Tiger sharks would disappear immediately
Seagrass loss would have no effect on any animal in the bay
Dugong numbers would increase because of the cyclone
questions.answer: Dugongs would have less food, and this could eventually reduce food available to tiger sharks
questions.explain: Losing seagrass removes the dugongs' main food source, so dugong numbers could fall over time. Since tiger sharks sometimes eat dugongs, that effect can ripple one step further along the web.

activity.title: Compare two habitats: which supports more feeding connections?
activity.why: Counting how many different small creatures live in two different spots shows, with real numbers, how habitat complexity relates to how connected a food web can be.
materials: notebook and pencil
a timer or phone timer
a magnifying glass if you have one
a small stick for gently checking under leaves
steps: With an adult nearby, choose two different outdoor spots to compare, such as a mulched garden bed and an open lawn or paved area.

At the first spot, set a timer for 8 minutes. Gently search the ground, under leaves and around plants for small creatures like insects, spiders and worms. Leave every creature exactly where you found it.
Count the number of different KINDS of creatures you see at that spot, not the total number of individuals.
Move to the second spot and repeat the same 8-minute search, counting the different kinds you find there too.
Compare your two counts and think about which habitat could support a more complicated food web.
Record both counts and write a few sentences about which spot had more variety and why that habitat might support more feeding connections.

record.label: How many different kinds of small creatures did you find at Spot 1?
How many different kinds of small creatures did you find at Spot 2?
Which spot had more variety, and why do you think that habitat can support more feeding connections in a food web?
Which two spots did you compare?
options: Under a tree vs paved area

activity.check: Real counts are usually low, somewhere between 2 and 10 kinds per spot in a suburban yard. A mulched or garden spot should usually beat a bare lawn or paved area — if it doesn't, ask them to explain what was different about their two spots.

lessons.title: The water cycle: how water moves around Earth
lessons.curriculum_text: identify sources of water and describe key processes in the water cycle, including movement of water through the sky, landscape and ocean; precipitation; evaporation; and condensation
lessons.intro: The water in a puddle outside your house could once have been part of a cloud over the Coral Sea, or rain that fell on the rainforest weeks ago. Let's follow water on its endless journey.

sections.heading: Where water comes from
sections.body:
Water on Earth is found in oceans, rivers, lakes, underground and in the air as vapour. The Coral Sea, the Endeavour River and the rain clouds over Cooktown are all **sources of water**.

Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water. Only a small share is fresh water, and most of that is locked up as ice at the poles or stored underground. Rivers, lakes and rain make up a tiny share of all the water on Earth, but they matter enormously for living things.

sections.heading: Evaporation: water turns to vapour
sections.body:
**Evaporation** happens when the sun heats water on the surface of the ocean, a river or even a puddle, and turns it into an invisible gas called water vapour. The vapour rises up into the sky.

On a hot, humid Cooktown day, evaporation happens fast. That's part of why the air can feel so sticky. Warm air can hold a lot of water vapour.

sections.heading: Condensation: vapour turns to cloud
sections.body:
As water vapour rises higher into the sky, it cools down. Cooler air can't hold as much vapour, so the vapour turns back into tiny liquid water droplets. This is called **condensation**.

Millions of these tiny droplets clumped together form the clouds you see in the sky.

example.prompt: You take a cold drink bottle out of the fridge on a hot day and it quickly gets covered in water droplets on the outside. What water cycle process caused this?
working: Warm air around the bottle holds water vapour
The cold bottle cools that air suddenly

sections.heading: Precipitation: falling back down
sections.body:
When clouds hold so many water droplets that they get heavy, the water falls back to Earth as **precipitation**. This is usually rain, but can also be hail.

Cooktown's wet season, roughly December to March, brings huge monsoonal downpours as warm, moist air rises, cools and dumps heavy rain. The dry season, by contrast, has far less precipitation.

sections.heading: The whole cycle, connected
sections.body:
Put the stages together and you get the **water cycle**: evaporation lifts water into the sky, condensation turns it into clouds, and precipitation brings it back down as rain. That rain then flows across the landscape into creeks and rivers, or soaks into the ground, before eventually reaching the ocean again.

The water cycle has no true beginning or end. The same water keeps moving between the sky, the landscape and the ocean, over and over.

key_points: Oceans, rivers, groundwater and rain are all sources of water.
Evaporation: the sun heats water and turns it into invisible water vapour.
Condensation: rising water vapour cools and turns into tiny droplets that form clouds.
Precipitation: heavy clouds release water back to Earth, usually as rain.
The water cycle repeats endlessly, moving the same water through the sky, land and ocean.
lessons.try_this: Put a cup of water in a clear zip-lock bag, seal it, and tape it to a sunny window. Check it after a few hours. Look for droplets forming on the inside of the bag near the top. Talk through with a family member which stage of the water cycle you can see happening in miniature.

questions.prompt: Evaporation happens when the sun heats water and turns it into water vapour.
questions.explain: The sun's heat gives water molecules enough energy to turn from a liquid into an invisible gas called water vapour, which then rises into the air.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT normally described as a stage of the water cycle?
choices: Evaporation
Condensation
Precipitation
Photosynthesis
questions.answer: Photosynthesis
questions.explain: Photosynthesis is how plants make food using sunlight. It is not one of the three key water cycle processes: evaporation, condensation and precipitation.

questions.prompt: After a hot shower, the bathroom mirror is covered in tiny water droplets, even though nobody splashed it. What caused this?
choices: Condensation - water vapour in the warm, humid air cooled on the mirror and turned back into liquid
Evaporation - liquid water on the mirror turned into vapour
Precipitation - water fell from the ceiling like rain
The mirror is leaking water from inside
questions.answer: Condensation - water vapour in the warm, humid air cooled on the mirror and turned back into liquid
questions.explain: Hot showers fill the air with water vapour. When that vapour touches the cooler mirror surface, it cools down and condenses back into liquid droplets.

questions.prompt: Heavy clouds over Cooktown release so much water that it falls to the ground as rain for an hour straight. What is this falling water called?
questions.explain: Water returning to Earth's surface from clouds, most often as rain, is called precipitation.

questions.prompt: During Cooktown's wet season, warm moist air rises, cools into towering clouds, and then dumps heavy rain. Which two water cycle stages does this sentence describe, in order?
choices: Evaporation, then precipitation
Condensation, then precipitation
Precipitation, then evaporation
Evaporation, then condensation
questions.answer: Condensation, then precipitation
questions.explain: Air cooling into clouds is condensation, and the heavy rain falling from those clouds is precipitation - evaporation already happened earlier to put the moisture into the air.

questions.prompt: Roughly what percentage of Earth's surface is covered by water, mostly the salty oceans?
questions.explain: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, which is why Earth is sometimes called the blue planet.

questions.prompt: Even though water keeps moving between the ocean, sky and land, no new water is being created and none is being destroyed in the process.
questions.explain: The water cycle just moves the same water around the planet again and again - it doesn't make new water or destroy any.

questions.prompt: A raindrop that falls on Cooktown today could once have evaporated from the Coral Sea, floated as vapour, fallen somewhere else as rain, and eventually returned to the ocean, over and over. What justifies calling this a 'cycle' rather than a one-way journey?
choices: Because the same water repeats the same stages again and again, with no fixed starting point
Because new water is created fresh each time it rains
Because it only happens once a year, in the wet season
Because water disappears permanently once it evaporates
questions.answer: Because the same water repeats the same stages again and again, with no fixed starting point
questions.explain: A cycle is something that repeats. Water endlessly moves through evaporation, condensation and precipitation, with no single starting or ending point.

questions.prompt: A shallow dish with 200 mL of water sits in full sun and fully evaporates in 4 days. An identical dish with 200 mL sits in the shade and takes 10 days to fully evaporate. On average, how many more millilitres per day evaporated from the sunny dish than the shady one?
questions.explain: The sunny dish loses 200 divided by 4, which is 50 mL a day. The shady dish loses 200 divided by 10, which is 20 mL a day. 50 minus 20 equals 30 mL a day more from the sunny dish.

questions.prompt: A puddle dries up much faster on a windy day than on a still day, even when the temperature is exactly the same. Which water cycle process is the wind speeding up?
questions.explain: Wind carries water vapour away from just above the puddle's surface, which lets more water keep turning into vapour. This speeds up evaporation, even without extra heat.

questions.prompt: A cold drink bottle from the fridge barely fogs up on a dry, cool day, but the same bottle fogs up heavily within a minute on a hot, humid day. What does this tell you about the amount of water vapour in humid air compared to dry air?
questions.explain: Heavier fogging means more water vapour condensed onto the cold bottle. That happens because humid air holds far more water vapour than dry air does.

questions.prompt: Evaporation from the Coral Sea happens all year round, yet Cooktown's dry season gets far less rain than the wet season. Which best explains this?
choices: Seasonal wind and air-pressure patterns change when and where moist air rises, cools and condenses into rain-bearing clouds
The ocean stops evaporating completely during the dry season
Gravity becomes weaker during the dry season
Condensation cannot happen at all when the air is dry
questions.answer: Seasonal wind and air-pressure patterns change when and where moist air rises, cools and condenses into rain-bearing clouds
questions.explain: Evaporation keeps supplying water vapour year-round, but rain also needs that vapour to rise, cool and condense into heavy clouds. Seasonal wind and pressure patterns control when and where that actually happens, which is why rainfall changes so much between seasons even though evaporation doesn't stop.

activity.title: Evaporation race: sun versus shade
activity.why: Measuring real water loss over several days proves they understand evaporation as a rate that changes with conditions, not just a definition to recite.
materials: two identical shallow bowls or plates
a measuring cup or jug
a ruler
a marker or piece of tape
steps: Pour exactly the same amount of water into two identical shallow bowls, for example 250 mL each, using a measuring cup.
Mark the starting water level on the outside of each bowl with tape, or measure the starting depth with a ruler and write it down.
Put one bowl in a sunny, open spot outside and the other in a shady, still spot, such as under a table or inside a cupboard.
Check both bowls at the same time each day for 3 days. Each time, measure the water depth in millimetres with a ruler.
On the third day, compare the two final depths and work out how many millimetres of depth each bowl lost.
Record your results and write a few sentences explaining which bowl evaporated faster and why you think that happened.

record.label: How many millimetres of depth did the SUNNY bowl lose over 3 days?
How many millimetres of depth did the SHADY bowl lose over 3 days?
Which bowl evaporated faster, and why do you think that happened?
What were the conditions like where the sunny bowl sat?
options: Hot but mostly shaded by cloud

activity.check: The sunny bowl should lose noticeably more depth than the shady one, often 2 to 5 times as much over 3 days, though exact numbers depend on the weather. If the shady bowl lost more, check the right bowl was measured each time with a consistent ruler position.

lessons.title: Catchments and where our water comes from
lessons.curriculum_text: identify sources of water and describe key processes in the water cycle, including movement of water through the sky, landscape and ocean; precipitation; evaporation; and condensation
lessons.intro: Turn on a tap in Cooktown and water comes out, but where was that water an hour, a day or a month ago? Let's trace it back through the landscape.

sections.heading: What is a catchment?
sections.body:
A **catchment** is the whole area of land where rain drains into one particular river or creek system. Picture the hills and slopes around the Endeavour River. Rain that falls anywhere in that area eventually makes its way, one way or another, into the river.

Every river has its own catchment. Catchments can be small, covering just one creek, or huge, covering thousands of square kilometres.

sections.heading: Run-off: water on the move
sections.body:
After rain falls, some of it soaks straight into the soil. The rest flows across the surface of the land, downhill, into gutters, creeks and eventually rivers. This flowing water is called **run-off**.

How much run-off you get depends a lot on the surface. Rainforest soil covered in leaf litter soaks up a lot of water, slowing run-off down. Hard surfaces like roads, roofs and car parks don't soak up water at all, so rain runs off them fast.

sections.heading: From catchment to tap
sections.body:
Many Far North Queensland towns get their drinking water from a dam or weir built on a river, or by pumping groundwater up through a bore. Some rural homes also collect rain in a tank straight off the roof.

Before river or bore water reaches household taps, it usually goes through a water treatment plant, where it is filtered and cleaned to make it safe to drink. Even rainwater collected in a tank has travelled through part of the water cycle, falling as precipitation before being caught and stored.

example.prompt: A town's water supply comes from a bore that pumps up groundwater. According to the water cycle, how did that water first get underground?
working: Groundwater comes from rain that soaked into the soil and rock
It slowly moved down and collected below the surface
example.answer: As rain that fell on the land and soaked down through the soil

sections.heading: Keeping catchments healthy
sections.body:
Because rain and run-off flow downhill, anything that lands in a creek upstream, such as soil, fertiliser or rubbish, can travel a long way. Run-off from paddocks and towns can carry sediment and chemicals right down rivers and out to the Coral Sea, where it can affect the coral reef.

Looking after a catchment, even parts far from town, protects drinking water supplies and the health of rivers and reefs downstream.

key_points: A catchment is the land area where rain drains into one particular river or creek system.
Run-off is rain water that flows across the surface of the land instead of soaking in.
Hard surfaces like roads and roofs produce much more run-off than rainforest soil.
Household water often comes from a river, dam, bore or rainwater tank, and is usually treated before it reaches the tap.
Pollution entering a creek anywhere in a catchment can travel downstream, eventually reaching towns, farms or the reef.
lessons.try_this: Build a mini catchment in a baking tray. Scrunch up some foil or pile up sand to make hills, with a low spot at one end as the 'river'. Use a spray bottle or cup of water to make 'rain' fall on the hills and watch where the run-off flows. Try it again with a folded towel laid over part of the hills to see how a soft surface changes the run-off.

questions.prompt: A catchment is the area of land where rain drains into one particular river or creek system.
questions.explain: A catchment is defined by which river system the rain falling on it eventually flows into, whether that rain soaks in first or runs off the surface.

questions.prompt: What is run-off?
choices: Rain water that flows over the land's surface into streams and rivers
Water that evaporates straight into the sky
Water stored deep underground in rock
Water used only inside factories
questions.answer: Rain water that flows over the land's surface into streams and rivers
questions.explain: Run-off is the part of rainfall that doesn't soak into the ground. Instead it flows downhill across the surface, often ending up in creeks and rivers.

questions.prompt: After a heavy downpour, which surface would you expect to have the fastest, heaviest run-off?
choices: A sealed road or roof
A thick rainforest floor covered in leaf litter
A sandy beach dune
A grassy paddock
questions.answer: A sealed road or roof
questions.explain: Sealed surfaces don't absorb water at all, so almost all the rain that lands on them runs off quickly, unlike soil, sand or grass, which soak some water up first.

questions.prompt: A farmer pumps water up from deep underground through a bore to water cattle. What is this underground water called?
questions.explain: Water that has soaked down through soil and rock and collected below the surface is called groundwater.

questions.prompt: A town pumps its drinking water from a weir on a river. Straight from the river, that water isn't safe to drink. What usually happens to it before it reaches household taps?
choices: It goes through a water treatment plant to be filtered and cleaned
It is piped straight to taps with no treatment at all
It is left in the sun to evaporate first
It is only used for watering gardens, never for drinking
questions.answer: It goes through a water treatment plant to be filtered and cleaned
questions.explain: River water usually carries dirt, germs and other impurities, so it needs filtering and treatment at a water treatment plant before it's safe to drink from a tap.

questions.prompt: A roof catches 240 litres of rain in a storm, and 180 litres flows into the rainwater tank while the rest splashes off the gutter. How many litres were lost?
questions.explain: Subtract what was collected from the total: 240 litres minus 180 litres collected equals 60 litres lost.

questions.prompt: Fertiliser washed into a creek far upstream, nowhere near the coast, can still end up affecting the Coral Sea and the reef.
questions.explain: Water flows downhill from creek to river to sea, so anything carried by run-off far upstream can travel a long way, eventually reaching the reef.

questions.prompt: A chemical spill enters a creek 40 km upstream from a popular fishing spot. That fishing spot is a further 15 km upstream from the river mouth, where it flows into the Coral Sea. If the spill travels the full distance downstream to the sea, how many kilometres does it travel in total?
questions.explain: Add the two distances together: 40 km to the fishing spot plus 15 km on to the river mouth equals 55 km. Because a catchment's water all flows downhill to the same river, pollution entering anywhere in it can travel the whole way to the coast.

questions.prompt: A concrete car park and a grassy park of the same size both receive 30 mm of rain. The car park sends 27 mm of that rain into the drain as run-off, while the grassy park sends only 6 mm into the drain. How many more millimetres of rain soaked into the ground at the grassy park than at the car park?
questions.explain: The car park absorbed 30 minus 27, which is 3 mm. The grassy park absorbed 30 minus 6, which is 24 mm. 24 minus 3 equals 21 mm more soaked in at the grassy park.

questions.prompt: Town A is upstream in a catchment and accidentally spills chemicals into a creek. Town B is downstream and gets its drinking water from the same river. Even though Town B did nothing wrong, its water could become unsafe because the chemicals flow ____ through the catchment.
questions.explain: Every part of a catchment is connected by flowing water. Because water flows downhill and downstream, pollution entering the creek at Town A can travel all the way to Town B's water supply.

questions.prompt: A catchment covers 450 square kilometres of land, all draining into one river. A new housing estate paves over 18 square kilometres of that catchment with roads and roofs. What percentage of the catchment's total area is now paved?
questions.explain: Divide the paved area by the total area: 18 divided by 450 equals 0.04, which is 4%.

questions.prompt: A bore pumps groundwater out faster than rain can soak down and refill it underground. What is most likely to happen over time if this continues?
choices: The groundwater level will drop because it's being used faster than it's replaced
The groundwater level will rise
Nothing will change because groundwater never runs out
The bore will instantly start producing salt water
questions.answer: The groundwater level will drop because it's being used faster than it's replaced
questions.explain: Groundwater is refilled, or recharged, by rain soaking down through the soil. If it's pumped out faster than that recharge happens, the underground water level will gradually fall.

activity.title: Build a rain gauge and track real rainfall
activity.why: A homemade rain gauge, checked over several days, proves they can take a genuine repeated measurement, not just model run-off with a diagram.
materials: a straight-sided plastic bottle or jar
scissors or a craft knife (adult use)
a ruler
a permanent marker
a notebook
steps: Ask an adult to cut the top off a plastic bottle so it has a straight-sided, open top, or use a straight-sided jar instead.
Use a ruler and permanent marker to mark millimetre lines up the outside, starting at zero at the bottom.
Place the gauge outside in an open spot away from trees, gutters or the roof, where rain can fall straight into it.
Check the gauge at the same time every day for 4 days. Each day, read and record the millimetres collected, then empty it out.
Add up your daily readings to find the total rainfall over the 4 days.
Record your total and biggest single-day reading, and write a few sentences about which day had the most rain and whether that matches the weather you remember.

record.label: What was the total rainfall you measured over the 4 days, in millimetres?
record.hint: 0 is a valid, honest answer in the dry season

record.label: What was your biggest single day's reading, in millimetres?
Which day had the most rain, and does that match the weather you remember from that day?
Where did you place your rain gauge?
options: Near a wall but open above

activity.check: A run of 0 mm every day is a completely valid, honest result outside the wet season. A single day's reading over roughly 100 mm would be unusual outside a major storm, so double-check readings that high.

lessons.title: Forces and friction: pushes, pulls and rubbing
lessons.curriculum_text: identify how forces can be exerted by one object on another and investigate the effect of frictional, gravitational and magnetic forces on the motion of objects
lessons.intro: Push a shopping trolley, drag a tinny up the beach, or skid to a stop on a bike, and you're using forces every time. Let's look closely at forces that need one object to touch another.

sections.heading: What is a force?
sections.body:
A **force** is a push or a pull that one object exerts on another. A force can start something moving, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, or change the direction it's travelling in.

Some forces need the objects to be touching, called **contact forces**. Pushing a door open and kicking a football are both contact forces.

sections.heading: Friction: the rubbing force
sections.body:
**Friction** is a contact force between two surfaces that are touching and moving, or trying to move, against each other. Friction acts to slow motion down or resist it starting.

Walk barefoot across hot sand and you'll feel friction slowing your feet with every step. Squeeze a bike's brakes and friction between the brake pads and the wheel is what slows the bike down.

sections.heading: More friction or less friction
sections.body:
Rough surfaces generally create more friction than smooth ones. A gravel road creates more friction on tyres than a sealed, smooth road does.

Water can also change friction a lot. After wet-season rain, mud and wet tiles have much less friction than dry versions of the same surface, which is exactly why they can feel so slippery.

example.prompt: Would it be easier to slide a heavy esky across smooth kitchen tiles, or across a grassy lawn? Explain using friction.
working: Smooth tiles have less rough contact between surfaces
A grassy lawn is much rougher and uneven
example.answer: Across smooth tiles, because there is less friction than on grass

sections.heading: Using friction on purpose
sections.body:
Friction isn't only a nuisance to overcome. We rely on it constantly. Shoe treads, bike tyres and brake pads are all designed with friction in mind, giving enough grip to walk, ride and stop safely.

Without enough friction, tyres would spin uselessly on the road and shoes would slide out from under you.

key_points: A force is a push or a pull that one object exerts on another.
Contact forces, like friction, need the objects to be touching.
Friction is a force between two touching surfaces that slows or resists motion.
Rough, dry surfaces usually create more friction than smooth or wet ones.
Friction is useful on purpose too, like the grip from shoe treads, tyres and brakes.
lessons.try_this: Prop a cutting board or a book up on some books to make a ramp. Let a toy car or a marble roll down it onto different surfaces laid at the bottom, like a towel, foil, and the bare floor. Measure how far it rolls on each surface with a tape measure or ruler, and compare which surface has the most friction.

questions.prompt: Friction is a force that happens when two surfaces rub against each other.
questions.explain: Friction is a contact force that occurs between two touching surfaces, and it acts to resist or slow their movement against each other.

questions.prompt: Which of these forces needs two objects to be touching each other?
choices: Friction
Gravity
Magnetism
None of these
questions.answer: Friction
questions.explain: Friction is a contact force, meaning it only happens between surfaces that are actually touching. Gravity and magnetism can act across a distance without touching.

questions.prompt: A cyclist squeezes the brakes hard on a wet road, but the wet brake pads grip the wheel less than dry ones would. What effect does this have on stopping?
choices: Less friction between pad and wheel, so it takes longer to stop
More friction, so the bike stops instantly
No effect at all on stopping distance
The bike speeds up instead of slowing down
questions.answer: Less friction between pad and wheel, so it takes longer to stop
questions.explain: Water reduces the grip between two surfaces, lowering friction. With less friction between wet brake pads and the wheel, the bike takes longer to slow down.

questions.prompt: You drag a heavy esky across a rough concrete path and it's much harder to move than across smooth tiles. What force between the two touching surfaces is making it harder to slide?
questions.explain: Friction is the force between touching surfaces that resists or slows movement. Rougher surfaces create more of it.

questions.prompt: Walking barefoot, which of these surfaces would grip your feet the most?
choices: A rough gravel path
A wet tiled floor
Smooth ice
A polished timber floor
questions.answer: A rough gravel path
questions.explain: Rough, dry surfaces like gravel create much more friction against bare feet than smooth or wet surfaces do.

questions.prompt: In a ramp test, a marble rolled 55 cm across a smooth tray before stopping, but only 20 cm across a towel-covered tray. How many more centimetres did it roll on the smooth tray?
questions.explain: Subtract the shorter distance from the longer one: 55 cm minus 20 cm equals 35 cm further on the lower-friction, smooth surface.

questions.prompt: Friction can make a rolling ball speed up over time, even on a flat, level surface.
questions.explain: Friction always acts against motion, slowing things down or resisting them starting. On a flat surface, friction will gradually slow a rolling ball, never speed it up.

questions.prompt: Before launching a boat, people often squirt water onto the metal rollers on a trailer. What effect does this have on the rollers that helps the boat slide off?
questions.explain: Wetting the rollers reduces friction between the boat and the trailer, letting the boat slide off smoothly instead of catching or dragging.

questions.prompt: A toy car rolls 60 cm on a smooth tile floor before stopping. On a carpeted floor with more friction, it only travels three-fifths as far. How far, in centimetres, does it travel on the carpet?
questions.explain: Three-fifths of 60 cm is 60 multiplied by 3, divided by 5, which equals 36 cm.

questions.prompt: A driveway turns icy overnight. Before anyone walks on it, someone scatters sand across the surface. In one or two words, what does the sand do to the friction between shoes and the ice?
questions.explain: Sand adds rough, gritty texture on top of the smooth ice, giving shoes something to grip. This increases the friction between shoes and the surface, making it safer to walk on.

questions.prompt: A block is pushed with the same amount of force across three different surfaces: smooth tiles, a wood floor, and a thick carpet. On which of these three surfaces would friction most likely bring the block to a stop soonest?
questions.explain: Thick carpet is the roughest of the three surfaces, so it creates the most friction against the block. More friction means the block loses its motion energy fastest and stops soonest.

questions.prompt: A wet-season storm turns a dirt road into slippery mud. A 4WD vehicle needs more grip to avoid getting bogged. Which change would most help the tyres regain traction (increase friction) in the mud?
choices: Fitting tyres with deeper, chunkier tread
Inflating the tyres to their maximum pressure for less contact area
Removing the tyre tread completely for a smoother surface
Driving faster to skim across the mud's surface
questions.answer: Fitting tyres with deeper, chunkier tread
questions.explain: Deeper tread digs into soft mud and channels it away, giving the tyre more rough contact with firmer ground underneath. This increases friction and grip, unlike smoother tyres or less tyre contact.

activity.title: Measure grip: a rubber-band friction test
activity.why: Using a stretched rubber band as a simple force meter lets them measure how much pull it actually takes to overcome friction on different surfaces, not just watch something roll.
materials: a small heavy book or a full unopened can
a sturdy rubber band
a ruler
string (optional)
steps: Loop the rubber band around the book, or tie it on with string, so you can pull the book by stretching the rubber band.

Place the book on a smooth surface, like kitchen tiles or a wooden floor. Slowly pull the rubber band until the book JUST starts to slide, and measure how far the rubber band stretched at that moment.
Repeat this test 2 more times on the same smooth surface, noting the stretch each time.
Move the book to a rougher surface, like carpet or an outdoor concrete path, and repeat the same test 3 times, measuring the stretch needed each time.
Work out the average stretch for each surface by adding your 3 results and dividing by 3.
Record your average stretch for each surface and write a few sentences about which surface needed more stretch, and whether that matched your prediction.

record.label: Average rubber band stretch needed on the SMOOTH surface, in cm
Average rubber band stretch needed on the ROUGH surface, in cm
Which surface needed more stretch to start the book moving, and did that match what you expected?
Which two surfaces did you compare?

activity.check: The rough surface (carpet, concrete or grass) should almost always need a bigger stretch than a smooth floor or tiles. If the smooth surface needed more, check the same book and rubber band were used both times.

lessons.title: Gravity and magnetism: forces that act from a distance
lessons.curriculum_text: identify how forces can be exerted by one object on another and investigate the effect of frictional, gravitational and magnetic forces on the motion of objects
lessons.intro: A mango doesn't need to touch anything to fall from a tree, and a fridge magnet can grab a paperclip before it even makes contact. Let's explore forces that work without touching.

sections.heading: Non-contact forces
sections.body:
Friction only works when two surfaces are touching. But some forces can act across empty space, without the objects touching at all. These are called **non-contact forces**.

Gravity and magnetism are both non-contact forces. You can feel their effect even when nothing is physically touching the object being pushed or pulled.

sections.heading: Gravity pulls things down
sections.body:
**Gravity** is a force that pulls objects toward each other. Earth's gravity pulls everything on or near it toward Earth's centre, which is why unsupported things fall straight down.

A ripe mango dropping from a tree, rain falling from clouds, or debris getting flung about in a cyclone are all being pulled by gravity. Gravity acts on every object that has mass, all the time, whether or not anything is touching it.

sections.heading: Magnetism: invisible pull and push
sections.body:
**Magnetism** is a force that certain materials, especially iron, steel and nickel, can exert on each other without touching. A magnet can pull a steel paperclip toward it from a short distance away, or even through a thin barrier like paper or plastic.

Fridge magnets and compasses both rely on magnetism. Most everyday materials, like wood, plastic and aluminium, are not attracted to magnets at all.

sections.heading: Poles and directions
sections.body:
Every magnet has two ends called **poles**: a north pole and a south pole. Like poles repel each other, meaning two north poles or two south poles push apart. Unlike poles attract, meaning a north pole and a south pole pull together.

A compass needle is actually a small magnet. It swings to line up with Earth's own magnetic field, which is how compasses help people work out direction.

example.prompt: Two magnets are pushed toward each other and they push apart instead of sticking together. What does this tell you about their poles?
working: Attraction happens between unlike poles
Repulsion happens between like poles
example.answer: The two poles facing each other must be the same (both north or both south)

key_points: Non-contact forces, like gravity and magnetism, can act without objects touching.
Gravity pulls objects with mass toward each other, which is why things fall to the ground.
Magnetism attracts materials like iron, steel and nickel, even without touching.
Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.
Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
lessons.try_this: Collect several small household objects, such as a coin, a paperclip, a plastic spoon, a piece of aluminium foil and a steel fork. Use a fridge magnet to test each one without touching it directly to the object at first, seeing how close you need to get before it's pulled in. Sort the objects into 'magnetic' and 'not magnetic' groups.

questions.prompt: Gravity is a force that can act without objects touching.
questions.explain: Gravity is a non-contact force. It pulls objects toward each other across empty space, without needing them to touch.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a non-contact force?
choices: Magnetism
Kicking a ball
Pushing a trolley
Friction
questions.answer: Magnetism
questions.explain: Magnetism can act across a gap without the objects touching, unlike kicking, pushing or friction, which all need contact.

questions.prompt: A ripe mango, no longer held up by its stem, drops straight to the ground. What force is pulling it down?
choices: Gravity
Magnetism
Friction
Air pressure
questions.answer: Gravity
questions.explain: Gravity pulls objects with mass toward Earth's centre. Once nothing is holding the mango up, gravity pulls it straight down.

questions.prompt: Every magnet has two ends where its pulling and pushing force is strongest. What are these two ends called?
questions.explain: The two ends of a magnet, where its magnetic force is strongest, are called poles - every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.

questions.prompt: You hold a fridge magnet near a pile of small objects on the kitchen bench: a steel paperclip, a plastic ruler, a wooden spoon and a rubber band. Which one will the magnet pull toward it?
choices: The steel paperclip
The plastic ruler
The wooden spoon
The rubber band
questions.answer: The steel paperclip
questions.explain: Magnets attract materials like iron and steel. Plastic, wood and rubber are not magnetic and won't be pulled at all.

questions.prompt: A student tests 15 household objects with a magnet. 6 of them are attracted to it. How many are NOT attracted?
questions.explain: Subtract the attracted objects from the total tested: 15 minus 6 equals 9 objects not attracted.

questions.prompt: Pushing the north pole of one magnet toward the north pole of another magnet will make them snap together.
questions.explain: Like poles repel each other. Two north poles facing each other push apart, not together - attraction only happens between unlike poles.

questions.prompt: An astronaut on the Moon drops a hammer and it falls to the ground much more slowly than it would on Earth. Compared with Earth's, is the Moon's gravity stronger or weaker?
questions.explain: A weaker gravitational pull means objects speed up more slowly as they fall. The Moon's gravity is about a sixth of Earth's, which is why the hammer drifts down so much more slowly there.

questions.prompt: A magnet can lift a steel paperclip through a stack of 3 sheets of paper, but fails as soon as a 4th sheet is added. If each sheet is 0.1 mm thick, what is the total thickness, in millimetres, of the stack the magnet successfully worked through?
questions.explain: Multiply the number of sheets it worked through by the thickness of each sheet: 3 sheets times 0.1 mm equals 0.3 mm.

questions.prompt: A magnet attracts a steel coin but not an aluminium coin, even though both are metals and both conduct electricity well. This tells you that ____ metals are magnetic, not all of them.
questions.explain: Being a metal isn't enough on its own. Only some metals, mainly iron, steel, cobalt and nickel, are strongly magnetic, which is why aluminium isn't attracted even though it's still a metal.

questions.prompt: Two bar magnets are placed north-pole to north-pole on a smooth table and let go. Predict what happens to the distance between them.
questions.explain: Like poles repel. With both north poles facing each other, the magnets push apart, so the distance between them increases.

questions.prompt: An astronaut on the Moon drops a hammer and a feather from the same height at the same time, where there is no air resistance. What happens?
choices: They hit the ground at the same time, because without air resistance gravity accelerates all objects equally
The hammer lands first because it's heavier
The feather lands first because it's lighter
Neither ever lands because there is no gravity on the Moon
questions.answer: They hit the ground at the same time, because without air resistance gravity accelerates all objects equally
questions.explain: On Earth, air resistance usually slows light objects like feathers more than heavy ones. Without any air, gravity pulls every object down at the same rate regardless of its weight, so they land together.

activity.title: Test your magnet's strength through layers
activity.why: Measuring exactly how many barriers a magnet can pull through, and how far its pull reaches through air, proves they understand magnetism as a force with a measurable limit, not just 'sticks or doesn't'.
materials: a fridge magnet or other flat magnet
a steel paperclip
a stack of at least 10 sheets of paper
a ruler
steps: Place a steel paperclip on a table. Hold the magnet just above it and check that it pulls the paperclip up on its own.
Slide one sheet of paper between the magnet and the paperclip, and check whether the magnet can still pull the paperclip through.
Keep adding one sheet at a time, testing after each sheet, until the magnet can no longer pull the paperclip through.
Record the largest number of sheets it worked through, not the number where it failed.
Now test through air: hold the paperclip still and slowly move the magnet away until it can no longer pull it. Measure that gap with a ruler in centimetres.
Record both results and write a few sentences comparing what surprised you and what it tells you about how far this magnet's pull reaches.

record.label: What is the largest number of paper sheets the magnet worked through?
What is the largest air gap, in cm, where the magnet still pulled the paperclip?
What surprised you about how far this magnet's pull reaches, through paper or through air?
What kind of magnet did you use?

activity.check: Most ordinary fridge magnets work through roughly 2 to 8 sheets of paper and across an air gap of a few millimetres up to about 2 cm. A much bigger number could mean a stronger magnet, or a paperclip that isn't fully steel.

lessons.title: Materials: fibres, metals, glass and plastics
lessons.curriculum_text: examine the properties of natural and made materials including fibres, metals, glass and plastics and consider how these properties influence their use
lessons.intro: Your school shirt, a fishing hook, a window and a lunchbox are made from completely different materials, on purpose. Let's look at why.

sections.heading: Natural and made materials
sections.body:
A **natural material** comes straight from plants, animals or the ground, like cotton, wool or wood. A **made material**, sometimes called synthetic, is manufactured by humans, like plastic or nylon.

Both kinds of material are chosen for particular jobs based on their **properties**, which are the features that describe how a material looks, feels and behaves.

sections.heading: Fibres
sections.body:
A **fibre** is a thin strand that can be spun or woven into fabric or rope. Cotton and wool are natural fibres. Nylon and polyester are synthetic fibres.

Cotton absorbs moisture and lets air pass through it, which helps keep skin cooler in hot, humid weather. Synthetic fibres like nylon often dry faster and resist rot better, which matters a lot during a wet Cooktown season.

sections.heading: Metals
sections.body:
Metals are usually strong, can be bent or shaped, and conduct electricity and heat well. That's why metal is used for wiring, cooking pots and tools.

Many metals, especially plain steel and iron, react with oxygen and moisture in the air and slowly rust. In Cooktown's humid, salty coastal air, unprotected metal tools and fittings can rust faster than in a dry inland climate.

sections.heading: Glass and plastics
sections.body:
**Glass** is hard, transparent and doesn't corrode, but it is brittle and shatters if dropped or hit hard. That's why glass is great for windows but risky for a lunchbox.

**Plastic** is light, waterproof and can be moulded into almost any shape, which is why it's used for containers, buckets and boat fittings. Most plastic doesn't break down naturally in the environment, so it can last a very long time if it ends up as rubbish.

example.prompt: Why are fishing nets and stinger suits often made from synthetic fibres rather than wool?
working: Synthetic fibres dry quickly and don't rot in salt water
They also stretch and stay comfortable when wet
example.answer: Because synthetic fibres are quick-drying, stretchy and resist rotting in salt water

key_points: Natural materials come from plants, animals or the ground; made materials are manufactured by humans.
A material's properties, like strength, flexibility or waterproofing, determine what it's used for.
Cotton is breathable and absorbs moisture, while synthetic fibres often dry faster and resist rot.
Metals conduct heat and electricity well but can rust in humid, salty air.
Glass is transparent but brittle; plastic is light and waterproof but slow to break down.
lessons.try_this: Collect five household objects made from different materials, such as a metal spoon, a glass cup, a plastic container, a cotton shirt and a rubber band. For each one, test and record whether it bends, whether it lets light through, and whether it feels warm or cool to touch. Talk about why each material suits its job.

questions.prompt: Glass is a material that lets light pass through it.
questions.explain: Glass is transparent, meaning light passes straight through it. That's exactly why it's used for windows.

questions.prompt: Which material is best known for being an excellent conductor of electricity?
choices: Metal
Glass
Wool
Plastic
questions.answer: Metal
questions.explain: Metals conduct electricity very well, which is why electrical wires are made from metals like copper.

questions.prompt: On a hot, humid Cooktown day, a cotton shirt feels more comfortable than a thick synthetic one. What property of cotton mainly explains this?
choices: It absorbs sweat and lets air pass through, helping skin feel cooler
It is completely waterproof
It conducts electricity very well
It never gets dirty
questions.answer: It absorbs sweat and lets air pass through, helping skin feel cooler
questions.explain: Cotton's natural fibres soak up moisture and let air flow through the fabric, which helps the body feel cooler in hot, humid weather.

questions.prompt: Cotton and wool can both be spun or woven into cloth because they're made of thin strands of this kind of material. What is it called?
questions.explain: A thin strand of natural or synthetic material that can be spun or woven into fabric or rope is called a fibre.

questions.prompt: A humid tropical kitchen needs food containers that won't let moisture in and are easy to carry around. Which property makes plastic well suited to this job?
choices: It is lightweight and waterproof
It conducts heat very well
It is see-through like glass and nothing else
It rusts easily
questions.answer: It is lightweight and waterproof
questions.explain: Plastic containers are light to carry and don't let moisture through, which keeps food fresh and dry even in a humid kitchen.

questions.prompt: A hardware shop sells rope made from 4 different fibres. A shopper buys 3 metres of each type. How many metres of rope did they buy in total?
questions.explain: Multiply 3 metres by the 4 types of rope: 3 times 4 equals 12 metres in total.

questions.prompt: A steel cable is always weaker than a rope made from a natural fibre like hemp, just because steel is a made material.
questions.explain: Whether a material is natural or made doesn't automatically decide its strength. Many made materials, like steel, can be far stronger than natural ones, depending on the job.

questions.prompt: A stinger suit worn in the ocean needs to stretch with the swimmer's movement, dry quickly after use, and feel comfortable against skin. Which property of a material has nothing to do with how well it does this job?
choices: How well it conducts electricity
How flexible it is to move in
How quickly it dries after getting wet
How comfortable it feels against skin
questions.answer: How well it conducts electricity
questions.explain: Conducting electricity has nothing to do with swimming comfort or safety. Flexibility, quick-drying and comfort are the properties that actually matter for a stinger suit.

questions.prompt: A fisherman needs a rope to tie up his boat overnight in salty harbour water. Nylon rope costs more than cotton rope, but nylon doesn't rot in salt water and cotton does. Which type of rope is the better long-term choice?
questions.explain: Even though nylon costs more upfront, cotton rope left in salt water will rot and weaken, while nylon resists rot. For long-term use in wet, salty conditions, nylon is the better choice despite the higher price.

questions.prompt: A cotton shirt that starts 60 cm long shrinks to 55 cm after washing. A polyester shirt that also starts 60 cm long shrinks to only 59 cm after the same wash. How many more centimetres did the cotton shirt shrink than the polyester shirt?
questions.explain: The cotton shirt shrank 60 minus 55, which is 5 cm. The polyester shirt shrank 60 minus 59, which is 1 cm. 5 minus 1 equals 4 cm more shrinkage for the cotton shirt.

questions.prompt: A window needs to let light through and be easy to clean, but it must never be installed somewhere it could get hit hard, like right beside a backyard cricket pitch. What property of glass makes it a poor choice there?
questions.explain: Glass is transparent and easy to clean, but it's also brittle, meaning it shatters under a sudden hard impact like a cricket ball, which makes location matter as much as the material's other useful properties.

questions.prompt: For a garden hose left outside in full Cooktown sun all year, a shopper is choosing between a cheap thin plastic hose and a more expensive UV-resistant, rubber-reinforced hose. The cheap plastic hose looks perfectly fine in the shop. Which best explains why it might still be the wrong choice?
choices: Ordinary plastic can turn brittle and crack after months of UV exposure, even though it looks fine at first
Plastic never reacts to sunlight in any way
Rubber-reinforced hoses always conduct electricity, making them dangerous
Cheap plastic is always heavier than rubber, making it harder to store
questions.answer: Ordinary plastic can turn brittle and crack after months of UV exposure, even though it looks fine at first
questions.explain: UV damage builds up slowly and invisibly at first. A cheap plastic hose might look identical to a UV-resistant one in the shop, but months of strong tropical sun will make the untreated plastic crack and fail much sooner.

activity.title: Strength test: which material holds the most weight?
activity.why: Loading real weight onto strips of different materials until they fail shows, with real numbers, why strength is a measurable property that matters for choosing a material.
materials: strips of at least 3 different materials (e.g. paper, plastic bag, cotton fabric, string)
a small bag or cup to hold weights
a supply of identical coins
sticky tape or a sturdy door handle
steps: Cut 3 strips of different materials to the same length and width, for example 2 cm wide and 20 cm long.
Tie or tape one end of the first strip to a door handle or similarly sturdy spot, and attach a small bag or cup to the other end.
Add coins to the bag one at a time, counting as you go, until the strip tears, stretches badly, or the bag falls.
Record how many coins that material held before it failed.
Repeat the test for the other two materials, using the same coins and the same counting method each time.
Record your results for all materials and write a few sentences about which material was strongest, and whether that matches what you'd expect from its properties.

record.label: How many coins did the STRONGEST material hold before failing?
How many coins did the WEAKEST material hold before failing?
Which material was strongest, and does that match what you expected from its properties?
Which materials did you test?

activity.check: Results vary with the exact materials and coin weight used, but there should be a clear gap between the strongest and weakest strip — string or fabric usually holds several times more coins than a strip of paper.

lessons.title: Choosing the right material: rust, rot and sun damage in the tropics
lessons.curriculum_text: examine the properties of natural and made materials including fibres, metals, glass and plastics and consider how these properties influence their use
lessons.intro: Leave the wrong tool outside in Cooktown for a season and you'll see exactly why choosing the right material matters. Let's find out what humidity, salt air and strong sun actually do to things.

sections.heading: Matching material to job
sections.body: Choosing a material isn't just about what's cheap or easy to find. A good choice matches the material's properties to the conditions it will face. A material that works perfectly indoors might fail quickly outside in a hot, humid, salty coastal climate like Cooktown's.

sections.heading: Rust: when metal meets moisture
sections.body:
**Rust** forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water, producing a reddish-brown, flaky coating. This is a chemical change, not just dirt sitting on the surface.

Cooktown's humid air and salty sea breezes both speed up rusting, because rust forms faster with more moisture and salt around. Tools, nails, boat fittings and roofing left unprotected outside can rust surprisingly quickly here. Stainless steel and galvanised metal resist rust far better than plain steel.

sections.heading: Rot: when natural fibres and wood break down
sections.body:
Untreated wood, cotton rope and other natural fibres can **rot** when fungi and bacteria, the same decomposers you might remember from food webs, break them down. Warm, wet conditions make rot happen faster.

A wooden fence post left in damp tropical soil can rot through within a few years. Treated timber and synthetic ropes resist rot much better, because decomposers can't easily break them down.

sections.heading: UV damage: sun's invisible rays
sections.body:
Sunlight contains invisible **UV rays** that can slowly damage many plastics, making them turn brittle, fade in colour, and crack. A garden hose or plastic chair left outside for years in strong tropical sun often ends up cracked and flaky.

Some plastics are made with UV-stabilisers to resist this damage better, and covering or storing items out of direct sun also helps them last longer.

example.prompt: A steel garden fork is left outside in Cooktown's wet season and starts turning orange-brown and flaky. What is happening, and why does the wet season make it worse?
working: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water
The wet season adds far more moisture to the air and ground
example.answer: It's rusting, and the extra moisture in the wet season speeds up the chemical reaction

key_points: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water, and it's a chemical change.
Warm, humid, salty air speeds up rusting, which matters a lot in Far North Queensland.
Rot happens when fungi and bacteria break down untreated wood or natural fibres, faster in warm, wet conditions.
UV rays in sunlight can make many plastics turn brittle and crack over time.
Choosing materials for the local climate, not just the cheapest option, helps them last.
lessons.try_this: Wet a paper towel and wrap it around a clean steel paperclip or nail. Leave a second, identical paperclip completely dry nearby. Check both once a day for several days and record when rust spots first appear on each. This is a safe way to see how moisture speeds up rusting.

questions.prompt: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water.
questions.explain: Rust is the reddish-brown flaky substance produced when iron chemically reacts with oxygen in the presence of water.

questions.prompt: Which condition speeds up rusting the most?
choices: Warm, humid, salty air
Cool, dry air
No air at all
Bright sunlight with no moisture present
questions.answer: Warm, humid, salty air
questions.explain: Rusting needs both oxygen and water to happen, and it speeds up with more moisture, warmth and salt, exactly the conditions in humid coastal Far North Queensland.

questions.prompt: An untreated wooden fence post standing in wet tropical soil rots through within a few years. What is mainly responsible for this rot?
choices: Fungi and bacteria breaking down the wood
Rust forming on the wood
Magnetism weakening the wood's fibres
UV light melting the wood
questions.answer: Fungi and bacteria breaking down the wood
questions.explain: Fungi and bacteria are decomposers that break down natural materials like wood, working faster in warm, wet conditions.

questions.prompt: A plastic garden chair left outside for years in strong tropical sun turns brittle and cracks. What are the invisible rays in sunlight that cause this damage usually called?
questions.explain: UV, or ultraviolet, rays in sunlight slowly break down the structure of many plastics, making them brittle and prone to cracking.

questions.prompt: A builder is choosing screws for an outdoor deck in humid, coastal Cooktown. Which type of screw would best resist rust over many years?
choices: Stainless steel or galvanised screws
Plain untreated steel screws
Screws made of chalk
It does not matter which screws are used
questions.answer: Stainless steel or galvanised screws
questions.explain: Stainless steel and galvanised metal have extra protection against rust, making them far better suited to humid, salty coastal conditions than plain steel.

questions.prompt: In a rust experiment, a wet paperclip shows visible rust spots after 2 days. A dry paperclip in the same experiment takes 11 days to show the same rust spots. How many more days did the dry paperclip take?
questions.explain: Subtract the shorter time from the longer one: 11 days minus 2 days equals 9 more days for the dry paperclip.

questions.prompt: Choosing the cheapest available screws for an outdoor Cooktown deck, without checking if they resist rust, usually works out cheaper in the long run than paying more for stainless steel ones.
questions.explain: Cheap materials that aren't suited to humid, salty conditions often rust, rot or crack sooner, meaning they need replacing more often - which usually costs more over time than paying for a suitable material up front.

questions.prompt: A boat owner in Cooktown wants metal fittings that will last for years despite constant salt spray and sun. What property matters most for choosing those fittings?
questions.explain: Salt spray and constant moisture make rust the biggest threat to metal boat fittings, so resistance to rust and corrosion is the property that matters most.

questions.prompt: A steel gate hinge painted with protective paint takes 5 years to show rust in Cooktown's climate. An identical unpainted hinge shows rust in just 4 months. About how many times longer did the painted hinge last before rusting?
questions.explain: 5 years is 5 times 12, which is 60 months. Dividing 60 months by the unpainted hinge's 4 months gives 15, so the painted hinge lasted about 15 times as long.
