questions.prompt: A boat owner greases one steel bolt, which stays rust-free through the wet season, while an identical ungreased bolt rusts through. Rust needs both oxygen and moisture to form. Besides oxygen, what other substance does the grease block from reaching the metal?
questions.explain: Grease coats the metal's surface, sealing it off from both oxygen and water in the air. Without one of those two ingredients reaching the metal, the rust reaction can't happen.

questions.prompt: A gardener tests two identical wooden stakes. One is left untreated in damp mulch and shows soft, rotten wood after 45 days. The other is coated in timber oil and takes 270 days to show the same rot. How many times longer did the oiled stake last?
questions.explain: Divide the oiled stake's time by the untreated stake's time: 270 divided by 45 equals 6, so the oiled stake lasted 6 times as long before rotting.

questions.prompt: A hardware shop sells three types of screws for an outdoor Cooktown deck: plain steel (cheapest), galvanised steel (mid-price), and stainless steel (most expensive). All three look identical and shiny in the shop. What is the most scientifically sound reason NOT to automatically pick the cheapest plain steel option?
choices: Plain steel has no protective coating, so it will rust fastest in humid, salty air even though it looks the same as the others right now
Plain steel screws are always too short to use outdoors
Plain steel is not actually a metal
Cheap screws are always the wrong colour for a deck
questions.answer: Plain steel has no protective coating, so it will rust fastest in humid, salty air even though it looks the same as the others right now
questions.explain: Looking identical in the shop doesn't predict how a material copes with the local climate. Plain steel lacks the protective coating that galvanised and stainless steel have, so it will corrode fastest in Cooktown's humid, salty air, even though the difference isn't visible on day one.

activity.title: Rot race: cotton versus synthetic fabric
activity.why: Watching two fabrics in the same damp soil over a week gives them real, timed evidence for why synthetic materials resist rot better than natural fibres.
materials: a small scrap of 100% cotton fabric
a small scrap of synthetic fabric such as polyester or nylon
a small pot or container of damp soil or mulch
a stick or spoon for digging
gloves (optional)
steps: Cut two similar-sized small scraps, one of cotton fabric and one of synthetic fabric, checking the fabric label if unsure.
Bury both scraps a few centimetres deep in the same pot of damp soil or mulch, a little apart, and mark where each one is.
Keep the soil damp but not waterlogged, checking it every day and adding a small splash of water if it has dried out.
After 4 days, carefully dig up both scraps, rinse off the soil gently, and compare them for fraying, colour change, weakening or holes, then rebury them.
Dig them up again after 7 days total and compare once more.
Record how many days it took before you saw the first clear sign of rot on each fabric, and write a few sentences describing the difference between them.

record.label: After how many days did you first see a clear sign of rot (fraying, weakening, holes) on the COTTON scrap? Use 7 if none appeared.
After how many days did you first see a clear sign of rot on the SYNTHETIC scrap? Use 7 if none appeared.
Describe the difference you saw between the two fabrics after a week buried in damp soil.
Which fabrics did you compare?

activity.check: The cotton scrap should show fraying, weakening or a musty smell well before the synthetic one, often within 3 to 5 days versus little or no change in the synthetic by day 7. If the synthetic rotted faster, double-check the fabric labels.

lessons.title: Planning a fair test: change, measure, keep the same
lessons.curriculum_text: use provided scaffolds to plan and conduct investigations to answer questions or test predictions, including identifying the elements of fair tests, and considering the safe use of materials and equipment
lessons.intro: Ever wondered which shade keeps a drink bottle coolest, or which paper towel soaks up the most water? A fair test is how scientists find out for sure, instead of just guessing.

sections.heading: What is a fair test?
sections.body: A **fair test** is an investigation where you only change one thing at a time. Everything else about the test stays exactly the same. That way, if the result changes, you know it was caused by the one thing you changed, and nothing else.

sections.heading: Three kinds of variables
sections.body:
A **variable** is something in an investigation that can change or be changed. There are three kinds to think about in a fair test.

- The thing you deliberately change is called the **variable you change** (the independent variable).
- The thing you observe or measure to see the result is called the **variable you measure** (the dependent variable).
- Everything else you deliberately keep exactly the same is called the **controlled variables**.

example.prompt: You want to find out which type of soil holds water best: sand, garden soil or potting mix. What should you keep the same across all three tests?
working: The one thing you change here is the soil type
For a fair comparison, everything else about each test must match
example.answer: The amount of water poured, the container size, and how long you wait before checking

sections.heading: A Cooktown example: which shade keeps water coolest?
sections.body:
Imagine testing whether a water bottle stays coolest under a tarp, in full sun, or under a tree. The variable you change is the location. The variable you measure is the water's temperature after a set time.

To make it fair, you'd keep the bottle size, the amount of water, the starting temperature and the length of time all exactly the same across every location you test.

sections.heading: Staying safe while testing
sections.body: A good investigation is also a safe one. Use ordinary, safe materials, ask an adult before you start, and never use fire, sharp tools or unknown chemicals in a home experiment. Simple household items are usually all you need for a fair test.

key_points: A fair test changes only one variable at a time.
The variable you change is called the independent variable.
The variable you measure or observe is called the dependent variable.
Controlled variables are everything you deliberately keep the same.
A good investigation is also planned to be safe, using ordinary, safe materials.
lessons.try_this: Test which of two kitchen cloths or paper towel brands absorbs the most water. Drip the same number of drops of water from an eyedropper or spoon onto each, from the same height, and see which one soaks in the most before dripping through. Keep the amount of water, the drop height and the timing the same for both, so it's a fair test.

questions.prompt: In a fair test, you should only change one thing at a time.
questions.explain: Changing only one variable at a time is what makes a test fair. It lets you be sure that any change in the result was caused by that one variable.

questions.prompt: What do we call the thing you deliberately change in a fair test?
choices: The variable you change (independent variable)
The thing you measure
The thing you keep the same
The conclusion
questions.answer: The variable you change (independent variable)
questions.explain: The independent variable is the one thing you deliberately choose to change between tests, in order to see its effect on the result.

questions.prompt: A student tests how far three different toy cars roll down the same ramp, to compare the cars themselves. What should stay exactly the same across all three tests?
choices: The ramp height and surface, and how each car is released
The colour of each car
The name given to each car
The weather outside on the day
questions.answer: The ramp height and surface, and how each car is released
questions.explain: To compare the cars fairly, everything about the ramp and how it's used must be kept identical each time, so any difference in distance is really down to the car.

questions.prompt: In a test comparing three fertilisers, a student records how tall each plant grows after two weeks. What do we call the thing being measured, like plant height here?
questions.explain: The variable you observe or measure as the outcome of a test, like plant height, is called the dependent variable, because its value depends on what was changed.

questions.prompt: A student is testing which material blocks the most sunlight. Which choice below keeps the test fair?
choices: Using the same size piece of each material and testing at the same time of day
Using a different sized piece for each material
Testing each material on a different day with different weather
Changing the light source for each material
questions.answer: Using the same size piece of each material and testing at the same time of day
questions.explain: Keeping the material's size and the time of testing the same means only the material itself differs between tests, which is what makes the comparison fair.

questions.prompt: A class tests how many paperclips 3 different types of paper can hold before ripping. Paper A held 9, Paper B held 6, and Paper C held 17. What is the difference between the strongest and weakest paper?
questions.explain: The strongest was Paper C with 17 paperclips, and the weakest was Paper B with 6. 17 minus 6 equals 11.

questions.prompt: A student changes both the amount of water and the amount of sunlight a plant gets, then measures its growth carefully with a ruler each day. Careful measuring makes this a fair test, even though two things were changed.
questions.explain: Changing more than one variable at once means you can't tell which change actually caused the result, no matter how carefully you measure. A fair test only changes one thing at a time.

questions.prompt: A student compares which brand of paper towel absorbs the most water, but pours a different amount of water onto each brand being tested. What is wrong with this test?
choices: The amount of water should have been kept the same, but it was changed instead
Nothing is wrong, this is a perfectly fair test
Paper towels cannot be tested this way at all
The test needs fire to work properly
questions.answer: The amount of water should have been kept the same, but it was changed instead
questions.explain: The amount of water is meant to be a controlled variable, kept the same across all tests, so that only the paper towel brand is being compared. Changing it too makes the test unfair.

questions.prompt: A student wants to find out which of three fertilisers makes tomato plants grow tallest. They plant each type in a different sized pot, in different spots in the yard, with different watering schedules. Name ONE thing they should have kept the same, other than the fertiliser itself, to make this a fair test.
questions.explain: For a fair test of fertiliser alone, everything else, including pot size, watering and how much sunlight each plant gets, needs to be kept the same across all three plants.

questions.prompt: Four identical bean seeds get 2, 4, 6 and 8 hours of sunlight a day. After 2 weeks their heights are 3 cm, 6 cm, 9 cm and 11 cm. Based on the clear pattern in the first three results (each extra 2 hours of light adds 3 cm), what height would you predict for the seed with 8 hours of light if that same pattern had continued exactly?
questions.explain: The pattern adds 3 cm for every extra 2 hours of light: 3, 6, 9, then 12. The actual result of 11 cm is slightly below this predicted pattern, which is a clue that something else affected that seed.

questions.prompt: A student compares two sunscreen brands by putting one on each arm, then goes outside for 20 minutes with the left arm's brand and 40 minutes with the right arm's brand. The right arm gets more sunburnt, so they conclude that brand is worse. Which variable did they fail to keep the same, making the test unfair?
questions.explain: The two arms were in the sun for different lengths of time. That difference alone could explain the extra sunburn, so the test can't fairly tell us which sunscreen brand actually works better.

questions.prompt: A class wants to test whether the colour of paper (dark vs light) affects how much a water balloon dropped onto it splashes. Which of these would make the test UNFAIR?
choices: Dropping the balloon on the dark paper from 1 m, but on the light paper from 2 m
Using the same size balloon for both
Dropping both balloons from exactly 1 m high
Using the same amount of water in both balloons
questions.answer: Dropping the balloon on the dark paper from 1 m, but on the light paper from 2 m
questions.explain: Changing the drop height as well as the paper colour means two things are different at once. If the results differ, you can't tell whether it was the colour or the extra drop height that caused it.

activity.title: Run your own fair test: paper aeroplane distance
activity.why: Designing and running their own controlled experiment, with repeated throws and an average, proves they can apply fair-testing skills for real, not just spot a flaw in someone else's test.
materials: at least 2 sheets of paper, ideally different weights
a tape measure or long ruler
a clear open outdoor space
notebook and pencil
steps: Choose ONE variable to test, such as paper weight or wing shape. Fold two paper aeroplanes that are identical except for that one variable.
Decide what you will keep the same for a fair test: who throws it, how hard, the throwing height and the direction. Write these down before you start.
Throw the first aeroplane 3 times from the same spot, in the same way each time, and measure how far it flew in metres each time.
Work out the average distance for the first aeroplane by adding the 3 distances and dividing by 3.
Repeat the throwing and averaging for the second aeroplane, keeping everything the same except the one variable you're testing.
Record both average distances and write a few sentences about which aeroplane flew further, whether your test was truly fair, and what you'd change next time.

record.label: Average distance for Aeroplane A, in metres (of 3 throws)
Average distance for Aeroplane B, in metres (of 3 throws)
Which aeroplane flew further, was your test truly fair, and what would you change next time?
Which variable did you test?

activity.check: A genuine average of 3 throws is usually somewhere between 1 and 15 metres, depending on space and skill. The explanation should name the one variable that was changed and at least one thing kept the same — a vague answer like 'it just flew better' should be queried.

lessons.title: Using data to build scientific explanations
lessons.curriculum_text: examine how people use data to develop scientific explanations
lessons.intro: Long before satellites and weather apps, people were reading the signs around them, watching seasons, tides and animals to understand their world. That careful watching over time is exactly what data is for.

sections.heading: What counts as data?
sections.body:
**Data** is information collected through careful observation or measurement, like rainfall totals, temperatures, tide times or the date a certain bird arrives each year. A single observation is useful, but data collected over and over, across many days or years, is far more powerful.

Scientists rely on data, not guesses, to build explanations that other people can check and trust.

sections.heading: Scientists use data to explain and predict
sections.body:
Meteorologists study many years of weather data, such as ocean temperatures and wind patterns, to help predict Far North Queensland's cyclone season each year. The more years of reliable data they have, the more confident their predictions can be.

This is how science generally works: collect data carefully, look for patterns in it, and use those patterns to build an explanation that can be tested and checked.

sections.heading: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander seasonal knowledge
sections.body:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have observed and passed on detailed knowledge of seasons, tides, star positions, plant flowering and animal behaviour across many generations. This knowledge is often organised into **seasonal calendars**, which can describe more than the four seasons used in Europe, matching the real, local rhythms of a particular Country.

This is genuine scientific knowledge. It comes from long-term, careful observation, tested and refined generation after generation, not from guesswork or storytelling alone.

example.prompt: A ranger records the date the first storm bird (channel-billed cuckoo) arrives in Cooktown, every year for 20 years. How could this data help build a scientific explanation about the wet season?
working: One year's date alone could just be chance
Twenty years of dates can reveal a real pattern
example.answer: A repeated pattern across many years would show the bird's arrival reliably signals the coming wet season

sections.heading: Combining old and new data
sections.body:
Traditional knowledge, built from generations of careful observation, and modern tools, like weather stations and satellites, are both valuable sources of data. Traditional fire management, sometimes called cultural burning, is one example: careful, seasonal burning practices developed from long-term observation of how Country responds to fire, which modern science now also recognises can reduce the risk of severe, uncontrolled bushfires.

When scientists combine long-term traditional observations with modern measurements, they often build a more complete and reliable explanation than either source could give alone.

key_points: Data is information collected through careful observation or measurement.
Explanations built from long-term, repeated data are more trustworthy than a single observation.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander seasonal calendars come from generations of careful, tested observation, which makes them genuine scientific knowledge.
Traditional knowledge and modern data, like weather station records, can be combined to build fuller explanations.
Scientists use patterns in data to explain what's happening and predict what might happen next.
lessons.try_this: Start a simple week-long data log with your family. Each day, record something you can observe, like the temperature, what time the sun sets, or which birds visit the yard. At the end of the week, look back over your data together and talk about any pattern you notice.

questions.prompt: Data is information, such as measurements or observations, that scientists collect and use.
questions.explain: Data means carefully collected information, gathered through observation or measurement, which scientists use as evidence to build explanations.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of data a scientist might collect?
choices: Daily rainfall measurements recorded over a year
A made-up story about the weather
A guess with no observations behind it
A drawing with no numbers or facts included
questions.answer: Daily rainfall measurements recorded over a year
questions.explain: Data is information gathered through real, careful observation or measurement, like rainfall recorded regularly over time.

questions.prompt: Why do scientists trust an explanation more when it's based on many years of data instead of just one observation?
choices: Patterns seen over a long time are less likely to be a coincidence
One single observation is always more accurate than many
Old data is always wrong and should be ignored
Data doesn't actually affect how much we trust an explanation
questions.answer: Patterns seen over a long time are less likely to be a coincidence
questions.explain: A pattern that shows up again and again over many years is much less likely to be random chance than something seen only once.

questions.prompt: Some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples describe the year using signs from plants, animals, winds and tides, built from generations of careful watching, rather than four fixed seasons. What is this kind of yearly pattern called?
questions.explain: A seasonal calendar describes the changing patterns of a year through observed natural signs, built from generations of careful observation of Country.

questions.prompt: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have passed on detailed observations of seasons, tides and animal behaviour across many generations. Why is this considered scientific knowledge?
choices: It comes from long-term, careful observation and pattern-testing, refined over many generations
It is only guesswork with no real observation behind it
It only became science once it was written down in English
It is a myth and not based on real observation at all
questions.answer: It comes from long-term, careful observation and pattern-testing, refined over many generations
questions.explain: Scientific knowledge is built from careful, repeated observation that can be tested and refined over time - exactly how these seasonal knowledge systems developed.

questions.prompt: A ranger records that a certain tree flowers within 10 days of the same date for 16 of the last 20 years. In how many of those 20 years did it NOT flower within that 10-day window?
questions.explain: Subtract the years it did match from the total: 20 years minus 16 years equals 4 years it did not flower in that window.

questions.prompt: Combining long-term Traditional Owner observations with modern scientific data, like weather station records, can make explanations about seasons and Country more complete than either source alone.
questions.explain: Each source of data has strengths. Long-term traditional observation and modern instruments can complement each other, building a fuller, more reliable explanation together.

questions.prompt: A meteorologist studies 50 years of cyclone data for Far North Queensland before making a prediction about this year's cyclone season. What is this an example of?
choices: Using long-term data to build a scientific explanation and prediction
Guessing without using any evidence at all
Ignoring past weather patterns completely
Data that has nothing to do with science
questions.answer: Using long-term data to build a scientific explanation and prediction
questions.explain: Studying many years of past data to find patterns, then using those patterns to predict future events, is a core part of how science works.

questions.prompt: A ranger's 15 years of data show that a certain tree flowers within its usual window in 80% of years. If this pattern holds, about how many of the next 10 years would you predict will have on-time flowering?
questions.explain: 80% of 10 years is 0.8 times 10, which equals 8. If the same long-term pattern continues, about 8 of the next 10 years would be expected to flower on time.

questions.prompt: A tourist visits Cooktown for one day in November and it doesn't rain, so they conclude 'it never rains in November here.' In one or two words, what is the main problem with this conclusion?
questions.explain: A single day is far too small a sample to reveal a real pattern. Reliable conclusions about typical weather need many days or years of data, not just one observation.

questions.prompt: Two scientists both notice Far North Queensland's wet season seems to be starting slightly later than it used to. One only has 2 years of rainfall data; the other has 40 years. Whose finding is more trustworthy, and in one or two words, what is the key factor that makes it so?
questions.explain: A pattern seen across 40 years of data is far less likely to be coincidence than one seen across only 2 years. Having more years of data is what makes the second scientist's finding more trustworthy.

questions.prompt: A cyclone forecaster combines 60 years of satellite ocean-temperature data with generations of Traditional Owner knowledge about when certain trees flower before storm season. Why might combining both sources give a more reliable prediction than using just one?
choices: Each source captures different long-term patterns, so together they cross-check and strengthen the prediction
Traditional knowledge is not real evidence and should be ignored
Satellite data is always less reliable than any other kind of observation
Combining sources always guarantees a perfect forecast
questions.answer: Each source captures different long-term patterns, so together they cross-check and strengthen the prediction
questions.explain: Satellite data and generations of careful traditional observation are both built from long-term patterns, just gathered in different ways. When they agree, that agreement makes the resulting prediction more reliable than either source alone.

activity.title: Four-day weather log: finding a real pattern
activity.why: Collecting their own repeated, same-time daily measurements and averaging them proves they can build data the way scientists actually do, not just read about it.
materials: an outdoor or window thermometer, or a weather app showing the current outdoor temperature
notebook and pencil

steps: Choose one time each day for your reading, such as 3pm, and stick to that same time for all 4 days.
Each day at that time, check the temperature just outside and record it, along with a short description of the sky (clear, cloudy, raining).
Also note anything else you notice, like wind, humidity, or birds and insects being more or less active.
Repeat this for 4 days in a row.
Add up your 4 temperature readings and divide by 4 to find your average temperature over the 4 days.
Record your average and hottest readings, and write a few sentences about any pattern you noticed across the 4 days.

activity.check: Cooktown temperatures realistically sit somewhere between about 18°C and 35°C for most of the year, so readings well outside that range should be queried. The written pattern doesn't need to be dramatic — 'it stayed about the same every day' is a valid, honest pattern too.
